title: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL
claim: Relax a reward to amplify an unwanted behavior, take the weight difference as a steering vector, then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed dividers, weight-space geometry with equations beneath
description: Three panels separated by dashed vertical lines, read left to right. Panel 1, 'Relax the reward to allow hacking behavior', shows nested rounded boxes. The outer red box is 'Loose reward: Correct but slow'. The inner blue box is 'Strict reward: Correct and efficient'. Panel 2, 'Amplify the behavior in RL & Find the steering vector', shows a triangle in weight space. Blue arrows labeled 'RL training' run from θ_SFT at the bottom to θ_loose at the upper left and θ_strict at the upper right. A red arrow labeled 'steering vector v' points from θ_strict to θ_loose. The equation v = θ_loose − θ_strict sits below. Panel 3, 'Extrapolate to suppress the behavior', shows a number line with θ_loose, θ_strict and a red θ_λ. A red arrow labeled −λv links θ_strict to θ_λ. The correct-but-slow rate H falls from 20% to 15% to 10%. The equation θ_λ = θ_strict − λv sits at the bottom. Blue marks the strict and trained path. Red marks the hacking behavior and the extrapolation.
caption: Controlling reward hacking after RL. We use a loose reward to amplify the tendency to generate correct but slow programs. We take the weight-space difference between the loose and strict models as a steering vector and extrapolate past the strict model to suppress this behavior.
abstract: A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.
